items.title: Self-Objectification Alters Brain Response to Media
items.snippet: How does the way a woman views her own body shape how her brain responds to sexualized images in the media? Researchers found that higher self-objectification is linked to dampened neural activity in aesthetic judgment regions.

items.title: Brain Speech Hub Builds a “Blueprint” Before We Speak
items.snippet: Textbooks have long taught that understanding speech and producing words happen in separate brain systems. A new study overturns that century-old model, revealing that a hub inside Wernicke's area builds an abstract "blueprint" for each word a quarter-second before we speak.

items.title: Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%
items.snippet: How do microscopic soot and wildfire smoke particles injure the brain? Combining health records from 500,000 people with inhalation experiments, researchers foundPM2.5 air pollution raises dementia risk by 25% and reprograms brain immune cells.

items.title: Why We Slow Down With Age: Brain Serotonin Blocks Movement
items.snippet: Why do we naturally move less as we grow older? Researchers discovered that the aging brain doesn't simply run out of fuel, instead, rising serotonin signaling acts like a biological brake on dopamine pathways that drive the urge to move.

items.title: Rice-Sized Wasp Brains Recognize Faces Just Like Humans
items.snippet: With a brain the size of a grain of rice, the Northern paper wasp can tell individual nestmates apart by their faces. Researchers identified the specialized wasp neurons behind this feat, revealing neural computations remarkably similar to human facial recognition.

items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
items.snippet: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
